questions.stem: A FortiGate on a supported SoC4 platform enters FIPS-CC mode without a USB entropy token. What should the engineer expect?

choices.text: The appliance silently skips entropy initialization and relies on the last boot seed.
choices.feedback: FIPS boot still requires an entropy source; skipping initialization would not satisfy the documented path.

choices.text: A FortiManager template supplies the entropy token during device installation.
choices.feedback: Firmware templates manage image versions and schedules, not boot-time entropy.

choices.text: CPU-jitter entropy supplies the built-in boot entropy source.
choices.feedback: FortiOS 7.2.6 documents CPU-jitter entropy and removes the token parameter on SoC3/4/CP9.

choices.text: The General Availability image automatically inherits the FIPS-CC certification state.
choices.feedback: Certification and image branch are separate; GA firmware is not interchangeable with FIPS-CC builds.

questions.stem: Boot self-tests pass, but the running build is from the ordinary GA branch. What conclusion is justified?

choices.text: The build is certified because every algorithm self-test passed during boot.
choices.feedback: Self-tests are one gate; certification status is tied to the approved image and release branch.

choices.text: The appliance should disable FIPS-CC until a USB token is installed.
choices.feedback: Supported SoC3/4/CP9 platforms use built-in CPU-jitter entropy rather than a USB token.

choices.text: The firmware branch can be inferred from the administrator's configuration backup.
choices.feedback: The backup does not identify the currently running signed firmware branch or build.

choices.text: The cryptographic mode is enabled, but branch eligibility still needs verification.
choices.feedback: A passing local self-test does not establish the image's certification or branch status.

questions.stem: A change window is planned to enable FIPS-CC, and the CLI warns configuration may be lost. What is the safest preparation?

choices.text: Enable the mode during peak hours, then compare VPN counters afterward.
choices.feedback: The documented change reboots the unit and may lose most configuration.

choices.text: Export configuration, verify the platform and image, and stage console recovery.
choices.feedback: The mode change is disruptive; backup and recovery access must precede the reboot.

choices.text: Install the newest GA image first, then enable the FIPS-CC flag.
choices.feedback: The matching FIPS-CC branch and its ReadMe must drive image selection.

choices.text: Remove the external entropy token and assume the saved configuration is preserved.
choices.feedback: The guide warns configuration can be lost during the mode change.

questions.stem: Fortinet publishes a security-hardening update for FIPS-enabled appliances. Which image-selection rule is correct?

choices.text: Use the matching FIPS-CC branch image and follow its release ReadMe.
choices.feedback: Fortinet publishes branch-specific FIPS images and directs administrators to each image's ReadMe.

choices.text: Choose the highest GA build number, regardless of certification branch.
choices.feedback: A higher GA build does not prove FIPS-CC branch compatibility.

choices.text: Keep the old image because boot self-tests are already passing.
choices.feedback: Security-hardening updates and branch support still require current release review.

choices.text: Select any candidate image that lists the same FortiOS major version.
choices.feedback: Candidate, certification, and patched status are branch-specific.

questions.stem: A scheduled firmware campaign is not visible in the GUI, but the CLI lists a profile under one ADOM. What does this prove?

choices.text: A FortiGate has already downloaded and installed the scheduled image.
choices.feedback: A stored profile is not proof that a device upgrade executed.

choices.text: The profile belongs to every ADOM because schedules are global.
choices.feedback: The profile database is grouped by ADOM; scope must be identified.

choices.text: The device database has been replaced by the firmware scheduler.
choices.feedback: Firmware profiles and device configuration databases are separate management objects.

choices.text: An internal firmware profile record remains stored for that ADOM.
choices.feedback: The diagnostic command exposes persistent per-ADOM profile data beyond the visible GUI list.

questions.stem: The stale firmware profile is confirmed in ADOM Retail. Which cleanup command limits the change?

choices.text: diagnose fwmanager profile clear
choices.feedback: Without an ADOM, the command clears profiles across all ADOMs.

choices.text: diagnose fwmanager profile clear Retail
choices.feedback: The ADOM argument scopes the clear operation to Retail.

choices.text: execute device database reset Retail
choices.feedback: This is not the documented firmware-profile cleanup command.

choices.text: diagnose fwmanager profile list Retail
choices.feedback: The list command inspects records but does not remove them.

questions.stem: Why is running the profile-clear command without an ADOM argument risky on a multi-tenant manager?

choices.text: It clears only profiles that have already completed their upgrades.
choices.feedback: The command scope is all ADOMs, not only completed tasks.

choices.text: It deletes device configuration revisions but leaves schedules untouched.
choices.feedback: The command targets firmware profile records, not device revisions.

choices.text: It can remove scheduled firmware profiles belonging to unrelated ADOMs.
choices.feedback: The Community tip states an omitted name clears profiles for all ADOMs.

choices.text: It changes the global firmware image repository for every managed device.
choices.feedback: The profile clear operation does not modify the image repository itself.

questions.stem: After a scoped cleanup, what evidence best confirms the intended profile was removed without affecting other ADOMs?

choices.text: Check only the device's running firmware version after a reboot.
choices.feedback: A device version does not reveal whether stale scheduler metadata remains.

choices.text: Compare profile-list output before and after, then inspect the task monitor.
choices.feedback: The list shows stored profiles; Task Monitor shows remaining scheduled work.

choices.text: Delete the ADOM and recreate it with the same name.
choices.feedback: That is unnecessarily destructive and does not verify the scoped cleanup.

choices.text: Rely on the absence of a GUI template row as the sole check.
choices.feedback: The problem itself is a possible GUI/database visibility mismatch.

questions.stem: After a FortiAnalyzer reboot, Device Manager shows Down, but the FortiGate reports registered/up and OFTP counters rise. What is the best first action?

choices.text: Allow the documented 10–15 minute status refresh interval, then recheck.
choices.feedback: The October 5 tip describes expected GUI reconciliation delay after reboot.

choices.text: Increase the no-log threshold immediately to six hours for every device.
choices.feedback: Changing thresholds can mask real silence and is not required for expected convergence.

choices.text: Re-register the FortiGate and rebuild every ADOM database.
choices.feedback: The transport is already active; these actions are not supported by the evidence.

choices.text: Disable OFTP and switch the device to scheduled upload mode.
choices.feedback: The current evidence shows the existing OFTP path is working.

questions.stem: Which command most directly shows that FortiAnalyzer is receiving logs at a positive rate?

choices.text: diagnose sys sdwan health-check remote
choices.feedback: That command inspects SD-WAN remote probes, not analyzer ingestion.

choices.text: diagnose fwmanager profile list
choices.feedback: That command lists FortiManager firmware profiles.

choices.text: get router info bgp network
choices.feedback: That command displays BGP route information.

choices.text: diagnose fortilogd lograte
choices.feedback: This reports the log receive rate at the analyzer.

questions.stem: A device uses scheduled uploads. Which default stale-log threshold does Device Manager use before showing Down?

choices.text: Six hours for scheduled uploading.
choices.feedback: The Administration Guide documents a six-hour default for scheduled upload mode.

choices.text: Fifteen minutes for all device logging modes.
choices.feedback: Fifteen minutes is the near-real-time default, not the scheduled-upload default.

choices.text: Thirty seconds after the last OFTP packet.
choices.feedback: The guide specifies time-based thresholds in minutes, not a universal 30-second timer.

choices.text: One day regardless of logging mode.
choices.feedback: The documented scheduled-upload default is six hours.

questions.stem: The GUI remains stale more than 30 minutes after reboot, and the OFTP packet count no longer increases. What should be checked next?

choices.text: Network path, device authorization, port 514, and fortilogd health.
choices.feedback: The recent tip recommends transport, registration, and receiver checks after the normal delay.

choices.text: The FortiAP DARRP optimization schedule and channel weights.
choices.feedback: Wireless channel optimization does not explain analyzer log transport.

choices.text: The FortiManager firmware profile database for the affected ADOM.
choices.feedback: Firmware scheduler metadata is unrelated to OFTP receipt.

choices.text: The Windows WEC ForwardedEvents subscription state.
choices.feedback: That is a FortiSIEM WEF collection dependency, not FortiAnalyzer OFTP.

questions.stem: A FortiSwitch 108 on 7.6.7 returns Broken pipe and crash logs repeatedly show /bin/sshd exits. What recovery path matches the documented workaround?

choices.text: Use console access to run execute ssh-regen-keys.
choices.feedback: Fortinet's Community tip gives this command as the workaround for the affected 108 versions.

choices.text: Reset every administrator password and leave host keys unchanged.
choices.feedback: The evidence points to the SSH daemon/key issue, not a credential-only failure.

choices.text: Disable host-key checking on all automation clients permanently.
choices.feedback: That weakens identity verification and does not repair the server daemon.

choices.text: Rebuild the switch's VLAN database before retrying SSH.
choices.feedback: VLAN state does not address the reported sshd crash.

questions.stem: After SSH keys are regenerated, an automation client reports a host-key mismatch. What is the correct next step?

choices.text: Disable strict host-key checking for every switch in the inventory.
choices.feedback: That removes an important server-identity control rather than validating the changed key.

choices.text: Assume the switch is under attack and factory-reset it immediately.
choices.feedback: A changed key is expected after the documented regeneration command.

choices.text: Keep the old key pinned and retry until the SSH session succeeds.
choices.feedback: The server now presents a new host key, so the old pin will continue to fail.

choices.text: Verify the new fingerprint through a trusted channel, then update known-hosts.
choices.feedback: Key regeneration changes server identity; clients must validate the new fingerprint.

questions.stem: Why does execute ssh-regen-keys terminate existing management sessions?

choices.text: It restarts the switching ASIC to relearn all forwarding entries.
choices.feedback: The command is an SSH service operation, not a forwarding-table reset.

choices.text: It reboots the entire FortiSwitch and clears its startup configuration.
choices.feedback: The documented behavior is an SSH server restart, not a factory reset.

choices.text: It disables all remote management protocols until the next firmware upgrade.
choices.feedback: The command regenerates SSH keys and restarts the SSH daemon.

choices.text: The command restarts the SSH server after replacing its key material.
choices.feedback: The CLI reference warns that sshd restarts and current SSH connections disconnect.

questions.stem: Which release is identified as fixing the FortiSwitch 108 SSH issue described for 7.6.6–7.6.8?

choices.text: FortiSwitchOS 7.6.5
choices.feedback: The issue is described in later releases; 7.6.5 is not the stated fix.

choices.text: FortiSwitchOS 7.4.3
choices.feedback: That release added the key-regeneration command, not the specific 108 fix.

choices.text: FortiSwitchOS 7.6.9
choices.feedback: The Community article explicitly identifies 7.6.9 as the fixed release.

choices.text: FortiSwitchOS 8.0.0
choices.feedback: The cited troubleshooting tip identifies 7.6.9 as the correction.

questions.stem: A managed FortiAP is expected to choose channels automatically, but no DARRP optimization occurs. What configuration should be checked first?

choices.text: The FortiNAC Physical Address Filtering group membership.
choices.feedback: That group controls host containment, not RF channel selection.

choices.text: The FortiManager firmware profile checksum for the AP's ADOM.
choices.feedback: Firmware profile metadata does not enable DARRP on a radio.

choices.text: The FortiAuthenticator LDAP CRL Check Mode.
choices.feedback: LDAP certificate validation is unrelated to radio provisioning.

choices.text: The per-radio darrp setting and attached ARRP profile in the WTP profile.
choices.feedback: DARRP is disabled by default and enabled under each radio.

questions.stem: An engineer enables DARRP and sees arrp-default-high-density applied automatically. What should be considered?

choices.text: Assume the AP has measured client density and selected the perfect profile.
choices.feedback: The profile is an automatic default, not proof of an RF survey result.

choices.text: Replace the profile with arrp-default because it remains the only supported option.
choices.feedback: FortiOS 8.0 replaces the old default with high- and medium-density profiles.

choices.text: Disable channel monitoring because DARRP runs only once at boot.
choices.feedback: DARRP uses scheduled optimization and subsequent monitoring behavior.

choices.text: Review whether high-density weights fit the actual RF environment.
choices.feedback: FortiOS 8.0 selects the high-density profile on first enablement by default.

questions.stem: Why does Fortinet recommend avoiding frequent DARRP optimization during business hours?

choices.text: Every optimization reboots the FortiGate wireless controller.
choices.feedback: The documented impact is channel change and client disruption, not a controller reboot.

choices.text: Channel changes can briefly disrupt connected wireless clients.
choices.feedback: The guide warns that optimization may change AP channels and interrupt clients.

choices.text: The ARRP profile deletes the SSID and recreates it on each radio.
choices.feedback: DARRP evaluates channel parameters; it does not recreate SSID objects.

choices.text: The optimizer disables DFS channels permanently after the first run.
choices.feedback: DFS behavior is a channel-selection caveat, not a permanent disable action.

questions.stem: A roaming complaint occurs after a channel change. Which evidence set best correlates the client experience with AP behavior?

choices.text: Only the FortiGate routing table and BGP neighbor summary.
choices.feedback: Those outputs do not show association, authentication, or RF roaming events.

choices.text: Controller debug, AP klog, client WLAN report, and an OTA capture.
choices.feedback: The Community guide recommends synchronized evidence from controller, AP, and client.

choices.text: Only the ARRP profile name from the WTP configuration.
choices.feedback: The profile shows intent, not the client's actual disconnect sequence.

choices.text: Only a screenshot of the Wi-Fi SSID and its VLAN assignment.
choices.feedback: SSID/VLAN state does not expose RF roaming and authentication timing.

questions.stem: A successful L2 poll completes, but hosts on secure ports do not appear in Ports View. What is the likely missing model capability?

choices.text: Reading static MAC-table entries through the secure-port model setting.
choices.feedback: Secure ports can turn learned entries static, which normal polling may ignore.

choices.text: Enabling BGP route suppression for the switch management subnet.
choices.feedback: BGP suppression has no relationship to FortiNAC MAC-table discovery.

choices.text: Increasing the FortiNAC EAP session timeout for all wired hosts.
choices.feedback: EAP state does not control whether static MAC entries are polled.

choices.text: Changing the switch to a different spanning-tree root priority.
choices.feedback: STP root selection does not enable static MAC-table visibility.

questions.stem: A disabled host record is deleted, but the endpoint remains blocked when it returns. What explains the behavior?

choices.text: The host's IP address is still cached in the FortiAnalyzer database.
choices.feedback: The enforcement list is stored on the switch by physical address, not analyzer logs.

choices.text: The disabled MAC can remain in the switch's secure-port list after deletion.
choices.feedback: The FortiNAC guide warns that deleting a disabled host does not remove the device entry.

choices.text: The device was automatically moved into the FortiNAC-F registry scan group.
choices.feedback: Registry scan policy does not explain a switch-side MAC restriction.

choices.text: The endpoint still has the old DHCP lease and cannot renew it.
choices.feedback: The documented secure-port behavior is based on MAC restriction, not lease age.

questions.stem: Why must the designated secure/static port be protected from ordinary endpoint access?

choices.text: The port becomes the switch's STP root and blocks all other VLANs.
choices.feedback: Secure-port enforcement is not an STP root-election feature.

choices.text: FortiNAC stops polling every other access port on the switch.
choices.feedback: The guide describes a restricted port, not a global polling shutdown.

choices.text: The switch stops learning MAC addresses on every production port.
choices.feedback: The feature restricts selected disabled MACs; it does not disable all learning.

choices.text: A disabled host connected there may regain network access by design.
choices.feedback: The secure port is the permitted restricted location for disabled MAC addresses.

questions.stem: Before deleting a disabled host from inventory, what should the operator do?

choices.text: Delete the switch model so the MAC list is cleared automatically.
choices.feedback: Removing the model is destructive and is not the documented cleanup path.

choices.text: Re-enable the host or remove the device-side restriction through the supported process.
choices.feedback: The device may retain the disabled MAC after the FortiNAC host record is deleted.

choices.text: Change the host's VLAN and leave its disabled record untouched.
choices.feedback: A VLAN move does not necessarily remove the secure-port MAC restriction.

choices.text: Run a full FortiAnalyzer SQL rebuild for the affected ADOM.
choices.feedback: The restriction is on the switch, not the analyzer database.

questions.stem: A registry value exists under the logged-on user's HKCU, but the Persistent Agent scan reports it missing. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The agent service runs under a different identity and does not see that HKCU hive.
choices.feedback: The Administration Guide explicitly warns that HKCU scans will not succeed for this reason.

choices.text: The scan engine can read only HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT and HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG.
choices.feedback: The guide lists several supported hives, including HKLM and HKEY_USERS.

choices.text: FortiNAC-F converts every HKCU scan into a REG_DWORD comparison.
choices.feedback: Hive selection and value type are separate scan parameters.

choices.text: The Windows endpoint must first register a new DHCP Option 82 lease.
choices.feedback: DHCP relay identity does not determine registry visibility to the agent.

questions.stem: A REG_DWORD compliance value is configured as hexadecimal text. What correction matches the guide?

choices.text: Change the hive to HKEY_CURRENT_USER and retain hexadecimal data.
choices.feedback: The hive does not change the documented decimal requirement.

choices.text: Select the Sets the value action for every DWORD comparison.
choices.feedback: The guide provides Match Value for comparisons and cautions about mutation.

choices.text: Enter the expected DWORD data as a decimal value.
choices.feedback: The FortiNAC-F guide explicitly requires decimal input for REG_DWORD.

choices.text: Convert the value to REG_SZ so the scan treats it as a number.
choices.feedback: REG_SZ is a string type and does not preserve DWORD comparison semantics.

questions.stem: A custom scan should report a mismatch but never alter endpoint state. Which action is appropriate?

choices.text: Match Value with the required comparison operator.
choices.feedback: Match Value evaluates the existing data without writing a new registry value.

choices.text: Sets the value, because it both compares and reports the existing value.
choices.feedback: That action can create or overwrite the registry value.

choices.text: Prohibit, because it always writes the expected DWORD into the hive.
choices.feedback: Prohibit changes failure semantics; it is not a value-setting action.

choices.text: General scan pass-through, because it preserves the current key.
choices.feedback: A pass-through setting does not perform the required registry comparison.

questions.stem: How do Prohibit and Severity differ in a registry-key custom scan?

choices.text: Prohibit chooses the Windows hive; Severity chooses the DWORD operator.
choices.feedback: Hive and comparison operator are separate scan parameters.

choices.text: Prohibit enables the Persistent Agent service; Severity restarts its process.
choices.feedback: Neither field controls agent service lifecycle.

choices.text: Prohibit can fail a host when the key is found; Severity grades a missing-key failure.
choices.feedback: The guide treats prohibited-key logic and missing-key severity as separate fields.

choices.text: Prohibit selects the registry value type; Severity converts hexadecimal data.
choices.feedback: Type and data representation are configured independently.

questions.stem: LDAP is reachable and the bind account browses successfully, but remote sync fails with unable to get local issuer. What should be examined first?

choices.text: The server's presented certificate chain and FortiAuthenticator trusted intermediates.
choices.feedback: The error indicates TLS chain validation failed before the sync could complete.

choices.text: The user's password-expiration policy in Active Directory.
choices.feedback: The failure is certificate verification, not an invalid user credential.

choices.text: The FortiPAM HA heartbeat interface and cluster priority.
choices.feedback: That is unrelated to remote LDAP TLS validation.

choices.text: The FortiGate SD-WAN service rule for the LDAP destination.
choices.feedback: The endpoint is reachable; the error is in the TLS trust stage.

questions.stem: What additional material is required when CRL Check Mode is set to All Nodes?

choices.text: Only the leaf certificate and the LDAP bind password.
choices.feedback: All Nodes checks every CA in the chain, not only the leaf issuer.

choices.text: A client certificate for every LDAP user in the directory.
choices.feedback: The optional client certificate authenticates FortiAuthenticator to the server, not each user.

choices.text: A DNS SRV record for every intermediate certificate authority.
choices.feedback: DNS service discovery does not satisfy the documented CRL requirements.

choices.text: CRLs for every CA in the chain and the full server chain in the handshake.
choices.feedback: The guide explicitly requires CRL coverage for every chain CA and full-chain presentation.

questions.stem: The LDAP server requires mutual TLS. Which setting addresses FortiAuthenticator's client identity?

choices.text: Trusted CA = All Trusted.
choices.feedback: That setting controls which server certificate authorities are trusted.

choices.text: CRL Check Mode = Leaf Node.
choices.feedback: That setting checks revocation of the issuing CA for the server certificate.

choices.text: Use Client Certificate for TLS Authentication.
choices.feedback: This setting presents a selected client certificate to the secure LDAP server.

choices.text: Protocol = StartTLS only.
choices.feedback: Protocol selects the TLS establishment method, not the client certificate.

questions.stem: LDAP browse works, but scheduled remote-user synchronization still fails. What distinction should be tested?

choices.text: Whether FortiSwitch has regenerated its SSH host keys.
choices.feedback: SSH server identity is unrelated to LDAP synchronization.

choices.text: Whether FortiNAC reads static MAC addresses from the switch.
choices.feedback: MAC polling is unrelated to remote LDAP user synchronization.

choices.text: The sync rule's own TLS, filter, mapping, and schedule transaction.
choices.feedback: A successful browse does not prove the separate sync workflow completed.

choices.text: Whether the FortiGate has a CPU-jitter entropy source enabled.
choices.feedback: FIPS boot entropy does not explain LDAP sync behavior.

questions.stem: After a primary FortiPAM fails, which data should not be assumed to exist on the new primary?

choices.text: The synchronized user and secret configuration.
choices.feedback: The guide says PAM configuration, users, and secrets are synchronized.

choices.text: Historical system logs and session videos written to the original primary's disks.
choices.feedback: The guide states logs and videos are not synchronized between HA nodes.

choices.text: The cluster name and shared HA password.
choices.feedback: Those are cluster configuration items, not local-only audit records.

choices.text: The passive node's device model and firmware identity.
choices.feedback: Those are required node properties, not session evidence artifacts.

questions.stem: The passive node takes the primary role after failover but privileged services remain suspended. What should be checked?

choices.text: The FortiAnalyzer Device Manager 15-minute log threshold.
choices.feedback: That threshold affects analyzer status, not FortiPAM failover maintenance.

choices.text: The Windows WEC ForwardedEvents log on the collector.
choices.feedback: WEF collection is unrelated to FortiPAM service resumption.

choices.text: Maintenance mode on the new primary and the documented resume action.
choices.feedback: The guide says the promoted secondary enters maintenance mode until an administrator resumes services.

choices.text: The switch's secure/static port list for the PAM subnet.
choices.feedback: Switch MAC restrictions do not control FortiPAM HA maintenance mode.

questions.stem: HA synchronization fails between a VMware node and a KVM node. What is the primary compatibility issue?

choices.text: The nodes have different numbers of licensed seats.
choices.feedback: The guide allows different seat counts; platform compatibility is the issue.

choices.text: FortiPAM does not support cross-platform VM HA membership.
choices.feedback: The Administration Guide requires VMs in one cluster to use the same platform.

choices.text: The primary has a different hostname from the secondary.
choices.feedback: Hostname is not the documented platform compatibility requirement.

choices.text: The nodes use different FortiAnalyzer ADOM assignments.
choices.feedback: FortiPAM HA compatibility is independent of analyzer ADOMs.

questions.stem: Why must HA priority and override be checked on each FortiPAM node separately?

choices.text: The settings are stored only in the FortiAnalyzer archive database.
choices.feedback: They are local HA settings, not analyzer archive metadata.

choices.text: Priority is derived from the number of active privileged sessions.
choices.feedback: The guide describes configured priority values, not session-count election.

choices.text: Those settings are not synchronized across cluster members.
choices.feedback: The guide explicitly requires manual, separate configuration of priority and override.

choices.text: Override is enabled only after the secondary enters maintenance mode.
choices.feedback: Override is an HA preference setting, separate from maintenance mode.

questions.stem: WEF events arrive in FortiSIEM, but the CMDB source is the WEC server. Is this necessarily a fault?

choices.text: Yes; every forwarded workstation must create its own CMDB device automatically.
choices.feedback: The Community tip explains that origin fields do not automatically create CMDB entries.

choices.text: No; the agent collects ForwardedEvents from WEC while origin hosts remain in event fields.
choices.feedback: The WEC is the agent host; original source identity is parsed from the event payload.

choices.text: Yes; WEF cannot preserve the original hostname inside the event.
choices.feedback: The original host can remain visible in parsed event attributes.

choices.text: No; FortiSIEM should discard the WEC and create no source device.
choices.feedback: The agent's transport source is the WEC, which remains the collection host.

questions.stem: A source computer is not represented in FortiSIEM. What should be verified before changing parser rules?

choices.text: That the FortiPAM secondary node has exited maintenance mode.
choices.feedback: FortiPAM HA state does not affect WEF collection.

choices.text: That the FortiGate FIPS-CC self-tests passed during boot.
choices.feedback: Cryptographic boot tests do not establish WEF subscription delivery.

choices.text: That the FortiAnalyzer Device Manager status threshold is six hours.
choices.feedback: Analyzer status thresholds do not affect WEC event forwarding.

choices.text: That its event actually reached the WEC ForwardedEvents channel.
choices.feedback: If Windows never receives the forwarded event, FortiSIEM cannot collect it.

questions.stem: Which agent-template event name is required for the WEF collection described by Fortinet?

choices.text: ForwardedEvents, entered in any letter case.
choices.feedback: The tip explicitly notes the event name is case-sensitive.

choices.text: Security, because WEF stores all events in the Security channel.
choices.feedback: ForwardedEvents is the WEC log name for forwarded events.

choices.text: ForwardedEvents, with the documented capitalization.
choices.feedback: The Community tip specifies ForwardedEvents as a case-sensitive event name.

choices.text: WindowsEvents, because the agent infers the collector log automatically.
choices.feedback: The documented template uses the exact ForwardedEvents name.

questions.stem: Which workload may still require native endpoint collection rather than relying only on WEF?

choices.text: File-integrity monitoring and telemetry not forwarded by the subscription.
choices.feedback: WEF covers selected Windows event channels, not every endpoint telemetry source.

choices.text: Standard forwarded Security events already present in WEC.
choices.feedback: Those are the intended WEF collection payload.

choices.text: Kerberos events already present in ForwardedEvents.
choices.feedback: The Community article lists Kerberos event IDs as examples of forwarded data.

choices.text: Events that the WEC subscription successfully writes to ForwardedEvents.
choices.feedback: Those are available for the FortiSIEM agent to collect.

questions.stem: A user receives 403 domain-fronting blocked; browser DevTools shows port 9443 and the SIA tunnel is active. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The explicit proxy and SIA tunnel are steering the same flow and SNI conflicts.
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents that proxy and SIA tunnel should not be used simultaneously.

choices.text: The destination web server has stopped listening on TCP/443.
choices.feedback: The 9443 proxy path and tunnel state point to a FortiSASE steering conflict.

choices.text: The FortiAuthenticator LDAP server rejected the user's certificate chain.
choices.feedback: LDAP trust is unrelated to the browser proxy and SIA path.

choices.text: The FortiGate failed to learn the remote site's BGP route tag.
choices.feedback: The reported symptom is a proxy/tunnel SNI conflict, not BGP route matching.

questions.stem: The endpoint is intended to use only the SIA tunnel. Which correction follows the Community troubleshooting tip?

choices.text: Change the destination server's certificate to a different SAN.
choices.feedback: The error is caused by duplicate steering and SNI rewrite, not the server certificate.

choices.text: Disable the endpoint's proxy/PAC settings and retest the tunnel path.
choices.feedback: The article recommends removing proxy settings when using the SIA tunnel.

choices.text: Increase the proxy listener port from 9443 to 443.
choices.feedback: Changing the port does not remove the conflicting proxy path.

choices.text: Disable all FortiSASE domain-fronting protections for the tenant.
choices.feedback: That weakens security and does not correct the endpoint steering design.

questions.stem: What does a 403 response alone prove in this scenario?

choices.text: Only that a request was blocked; correlate port, PAC, tunnel, and SNI.
choices.feedback: The Community tip requires path evidence to identify the domain-fronting conflict.

choices.text: That the destination server is unavailable for every endpoint.
choices.feedback: A FortiSASE policy block does not establish destination availability.

choices.text: That the endpoint has an invalid FortiClient license.
choices.feedback: The cited root cause is simultaneous proxy and SIA steering.

choices.text: That the user's identity failed SAML authentication.
choices.feedback: The error occurs at the traffic steering/SNI boundary, not necessarily identity login.

questions.stem: Which evidence set best isolates the duplicate steering path?

choices.text: FortiPAM session recording quota and FortiAnalyzer archive age.
choices.feedback: Those systems do not participate in FortiSASE browser steering.

choices.text: FortiNAC secure-port MAC list and switch L2 poll result.
choices.feedback: Those outputs describe wired host containment, not web proxy traffic.

choices.text: FortiGate boot entropy source and FIPS self-test status.
choices.feedback: Cryptographic boot state does not show PAC or SIA flow selection.

choices.text: Browser request port, PAC decision, SIA tunnel state, and observed SNI.
choices.feedback: Those observations distinguish the explicit-proxy path from the SIA tunnel.

questions.stem: One of two overlay members to a spoke fails, but the other continues passing remote SLA probes. Should the hub suppress the spoke route?

choices.text: Yes; any single failed tunnel immediately raises MED to 999.
choices.feedback: The guide describes suppression after every member in the health check is dead.

choices.text: No; suppression is intended when all monitored members to the spoke are dead.
choices.feedback: The feature distinguishes one failed member from all-member remote probe failure.

choices.text: Yes; the BGP peer must be reset whenever one SLA probe is lost.
choices.feedback: The mechanism changes route attributes based on aggregate member state.

choices.text: No; remote SLA probes are unrelated to BGP route advertisement.
choices.feedback: The feature explicitly links remote health-check state to BGP route suppression.

questions.stem: All hub-to-spoke members are dead. Which combination enables the intended route-suppression transaction?

choices.text: Enable BGP route tags and use an inbound firewall address object only.
choices.feedback: Route-tag destination classification is a different mechanism from suppression state.

choices.text: Disable remote probes and lower MED on the failed hub's routes.
choices.feedback: Without probes, the hub cannot determine that all overlay members are dead.

choices.text: Restart the spoke BGP process and clear the SD-WAN member table.
choices.feedback: The documented feature uses health-check state and route-map-out behavior.

choices.text: Enable update-bgp-route and use an outbound route-map matching suppression.
choices.feedback: The health-check marks route state and the route-map translates it into BGP attributes.

questions.stem: An external peer still prefers the dead hub after suppression. What should be checked on the BGP advertisement?

choices.text: The spoke advertises a lower MED for the failed hub's path.
choices.feedback: A lower MED makes that path more attractive, not less.

choices.text: The route-map rewrites the destination prefix to a null route.
choices.feedback: The documented mechanism adjusts MED based on suppression state.

choices.text: The route-map sets a higher MED for suppressed routes and the peer preserves it.
choices.feedback: The guide uses a high MED for suppressed routes and requires MED preservation toward peers.

choices.text: The hub disables every BGP neighbor until the tunnel returns.
choices.feedback: The feature preserves BGP peering and changes route preference.

questions.stem: Which command output directly exposes alive-count and route-suppressed state for dynamic BGP peers?

choices.text: diagnose fortilogd lograte
choices.feedback: That command reports FortiAnalyzer log ingestion rate.

choices.text: diagnose sys link-monitor dynamic-bgp-peers
choices.feedback: This command displays the peer's alive count and suppression state.

choices.text: diagnose fwmanager profile list
choices.feedback: That command lists FortiManager firmware profile records.

choices.text: diagnose wireless-controller wlac show all
choices.feedback: That command displays wireless-controller station information.

questions.stem: A green management status appears after a reboot, but the engineer needs proof of application data processing. Which principle applies to both FortiAnalyzer and FortiSIEM?

choices.text: Separate transport/collector health from successful parsing, indexing, and query visibility.
choices.feedback: Connection or receipt counters do not prove downstream analytics or parsing completed.

choices.text: Treat every green connection indicator as proof that all events are searchable.
choices.feedback: Both systems have separate ingestion, parsing, and display stages.

choices.text: Increase all status timeouts until the user interface shows no warnings.
choices.feedback: Changing timeouts can hide gaps without proving processing success.

choices.text: Rebuild every database before checking packet or event counters.
choices.feedback: Evidence should isolate the failing stage before disruptive rebuilds.

questions.stem: A troubleshooting command changes cryptographic identity or routing preference. What should the change plan preserve?

choices.text: Only the command transcript, because the system restores old state automatically.
choices.feedback: Neither operation automatically restores the previous identity or routing state.

choices.text: A screenshot of the GUI, with no peer-side verification.
choices.feedback: Both changes need evidence from clients or external routing peers.

choices.text: Before/after evidence, rollback path, scope, and an independent validation test.
choices.feedback: Host-key regeneration and BGP route suppression both change trust or path behavior.

choices.text: The full configuration reset, because narrow rollback is unsupported.
choices.feedback: Both mechanisms can be changed with scoped, planned operations.
